ready2_open_rewrite.final_cot: Image description: The figure decomposes a 3-pyramid into 3 layers of balls: on the left is the bottom layer, with 6 balls arranged in a triangle of side length 3; in the middle is the second layer, with 3 balls arranged in a triangle of side length 2; further to the right is the 1 ball of the top layer. The right side of the arrow shows these layers stacked together to form a tetrahedron-shaped pile of balls. Reasoning: Similarly, an 8-pyramid can be regarded as a tetrahedral pile of balls whose triangular layers have side lengths 8,7,6,5,4,3,2,1 in order. Use tetrahedral coordinates relative to the four faces to represent each ball; the balls on the outside are the balls that lie on at least one boundary face. After removing all outside balls, the remaining balls must be at least one layer away from all four faces. That is, one layer is cut away from each of the four faces, and the side length of the tetrahedron decreases by 4. Therefore the side length of the remaining inner part of the 8-pyramid is 8-4=4, and it is still the same kind of pyramid-shaped pile of balls.

method.method_draft: First describe the image: it shows a 3-pyramid made by stacking triangular layers of balls: a bottom triangular layer with side length 3, a middle triangular layer with side length 2, and a top single ball, producing a tetrahedral pile. From the text, generalize that an 8-pyramid is the analogous tetrahedral stack with triangular layers of side lengths 8, 7, 6, ..., 1. Model each ball in an n-pyramid by tetrahedral/barycentric coordinates relative to the four faces. A ball is outside exactly when it lies on at least one of the four boundary faces. After removing all outside balls, only balls with positive distance from every face remain. Subtracting one layer from each of the four faces reduces the side length by 4, so the inside of an 8-pyramid has side length 8 - 4 = 4. Therefore the remaining balls form a 4-pyramid.
